text: Moment arms relate muscle force to joint torque. For a fixed-axis joint, the signed moment arm is $r_{\mathrm{m}}=\hat{\mathbf{a}}\cdot(\mathbf{r}\times\hat{\mathbf{u}})$, where $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$ is the joint-axis direction, $\mathbf{r}$ locates a point on the muscle's line of action relative to the joint, and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ is the force direction \citep{brand_model_1982}. The tendon-excursion method instead evaluates the sensitivity of musculotendon length to the joint coordinate, with sign determined by the coordinate and force conventions \citep{menegaldo_moment_2004}. For multiarticular muscles, the result also depends on adjacent-joint configurations \citep{zajac_determining_1989, young_analyzing_2019}. OpenSim uses length sensitivities, so the reference moment arms in this dissertation are properties of the Gait2392-derived geometry \citep{delp_opensim_2007, seth_opensim_2018}. Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} compares the robot's resulting torque predictions with test-stand measurements.

text: Knee modeling requires particular care because the instantaneous center of rotation changes with flexion. Four-bar descriptions reproduce this behavior through linkage geometry \citep{romero_four-bar_2020, steele_biomimetic_2018}. Gait2392 instead prescribes planar translations as functions of knee flexion \citep{yamaguchi_planar_1989}. These different kinematics produce different moment arms for the same nominal attachment locations. Joint-coordinate conventions must therefore be stated consistently when comparing models and measurements \citep{wu_isb_2002}. Gait2392 provides the human reference in this dissertation, while Steele's four-bar mechanism supplies the physical robot knee.

text: Designing a biomimetic leg requires a quantitative benchmark of human muscle--joint behavior. This dissertation uses OpenSim \citep{delp_opensim_2007, seth_opensim_2011, seth_opensim_2018} and the Gait2392 model, named for its 23 degrees of freedom and 92 musculotendon actuators. Gait2392 descends from the interactive lower-extremity model of \citet{delp_interactive_1990} and includes musculoskeletal geometry from \citet{hoy_musculoskeletal_1990} and planar knee kinematics from \citet{yamaguchi_planar_1989}; related lower-limb models of the same family are characterized and validated by \citet{arnold_model_2010}. Muscle moment arms, force-generating properties, and functional roles in such models have been characterized extensively \citep{zajac_determining_1989, brand_model_1982, menegaldo_moment_2004, millard_flexing_2013, sherman_what_2013, suderman_moving_2012}, and standard reporting conventions for kinematics and joint mechanics are established by the International Society of Biomechanics \citep{wu_for_1995, wu_isb_2002, wu_isb_2005, derrick_isb_2020}.

text: The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed on healthy humans. Invasive intervention on the human neuromuscular system is limited to clinical populations, is tightly constrained by ethics review, and permits neither the within-subject control nor the reversibility that neuromechanical hypotheses demand. The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. Robotic and computational models allow proposed neural interventions to be tested under controlled conditions before corresponding animal experiments are considered. The same model and initial conditions can be reused across interventions to isolate the effect of a changed pathway. Repeating a model does not create independent biological subjects, and its relevance to animal experiments depends on validation against biological observations.

text: The source represents patella motion through muscle insertion locations that vary with knee angle. In the converted model, limits on the joints representing these moving path points conflicted with their coupling constraints. Removing those conflicting limits allowed the coupled path points to follow their prescribed trajectories. The rectus femoris path also required a patella-tracking via point to restore its knee-extension action. Explicit collision pairs introduced unwanted contacts, so contact was restricted to the foot--ground pairs. The anatomical joint limits also had to be re-enabled; these driver joints were treated separately from the coupled path-point joints. Passive joint torques supplemented the joint behavior. These repairs explain why conversion needed checks beyond successful loading: a model could load while producing an incorrect torque direction or unintended contact force.

text: The actuator and torque models of Chapters~\ref{ch:muscles} and~\ref{ch:torque} describe actuator force and joint torque. This chapter develops a simulation framework in which neural controllers can drive the Gait2392 musculoskeletal model and separate BPA-actuated models, receive sensory feedback, and be tested under specified support and disturbance conditions. The contribution is the implemented framework and its demonstrated tests; unsupported walking remains an open control problem.

original_highlight: Historical exact highlight (22 Oct. capture): Two definitions cover most of the neuroscience vocabulary used below. First, the locomotor controller is a two-level central pattern generator: a rhythm generator sets the timing of the step cycle, and a pattern-formation layer shapes that timing into phase-appropriate activation of antagonist muscle groups \citep{rybak_modelling_2006}. Each leg's rhythm generator is a pair of mutually inhibiting antagonist populations, one extensor and one flexor, so that only one is strongly active at a time. Second, in the non-spiking (graded) formulation used for most of this work, each neuron is electrically a nonlinear RC circuit: synaptic current charges a membrane capacitance through a leak conductance, and the resulting membrane voltage, tens of millivolts, is both the neuron's state and its output \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Graded chemical synapses couple these units: a depolarized presynaptic cell opens a conductance in the postsynaptic membrane whose sign makes the connection excitatory or inhibitory. The sensory channels that close the loop are the muscle afferents, Ia signaling muscle length and velocity, Ib signaling muscle force, and group II signaling length, together with heel and toe contact sensors.

text: The framework is evaluated at three levels. Circuit tests ask whether a controller produces the intended neural response. Interface tests ask whether activation, muscle force, and sensory measurements pass correctly between the neural and mechanical models. They establish a working basis for controlled neuromechanical experiments while identifying the balance, model-transfer, and controller-tuning problems that remain.

text: The MuJoCo simulations allow mechanical support to be specified independently of the neural controller. A virtual harness applies forces and torques to the body: it can hold the model above the ground, lower it into contact, retain vertical support, or constrain selected directions of translation and rotation. These settings represent different experimental conditions. Suspended motion tests whether the controller and actuators can move the limbs, whereas supported ground contact adds loading and sensory feedback. Progression with retained support is reported separately from unsupported walking.

text: Existing tools supply the components of this framework. OpenSim provides musculoskeletal geometry, MyoConverter translates that geometry to MuJoCo, and SNS-Toolbox supplies neuron and synapse models \citep{delp_opensim_2007, caggiano_myosuite_2022, todorov_mujoco_2012, nourse_sns_2023}. MuJoCo supports scripted dynamics, contact, and repeated evaluations; the version used here models rigid tendons. Simulink supplies graphical circuit assembly, and Simscape Multibody supplies mechanical imports, including CAD-derived mechanisms. AnimatLab contains the original walker and reference circuits. My contribution connects these components through the model conversions, actuator calculations, circuit implementations, and tests described below.
